meta.title: Mumbaicha Peshwa
meta.marathi: मुंबईचा पेशवा - बाळ गोपाळ मित्र मंडळ
meta.foundedNote: 1989 is stated by the mandal and corroborated by contemporary PTI and Marathi reporting. The names Vile Parlecha Peshwa and Mumbaicha Peshwa are later identities, not separate founding dates.
meta.intro: Mumbaicha Peshwa is Bal Gopal Mitra Mandal's public Ganesh festival in Vile Parle East. The mandal began in 1989 and describes an origin among schoolchildren assisted by older residents. Its later history centres on large paper-based Ganesh forms, with materials and supporting figures changing between years. Social themes appear in the surrounding scenery and performances. Contemporary Marathi and English reports document particular commissions, helping separate the festival's general reputation from the actual form and materials reported for each year.

sections.title: Children, neighbours and a changing name

paragraphs.text: The mandal's Marathi history dates its establishment to 1989 and recalls schoolchildren pooling pocket money, with older residents, to buy and install an idol. It says volunteers adopted the name Vile Parlecha Peshwa in 2001 and Mumbaicha Peshwa in 2016. These are stages in one organisation's identity. The founding year is also reported by PTI in 2024 and Loksatta in 2025.

The same institutional account describes moving-picture presentations and social work, including blood donation, educational assistance and help for vulnerable households. These statements provide a community perspective, while the dates and outcomes of individual initiatives still need original records. The homepage's narrative refers to 2022; its anniversary language should not be mistaken for a current annual count.

sections.title: A material experiment with annual variations

paragraphs.text: The mandal places its tissue-paper idol practice from 2008, a date also reported in Marathi coverage. In the 2024 PTI report, committee member Sunil Mayekar described a 23-foot figure made with used temple flowers and tissue paper. The report names Digambar Mayekar and Rajesh Digambar Mayekar as sculptors and describes four mice supporting Ganesh's palanquin. Material and size claims remain specific to that reported commission.

Ashutosh M Shukla's 2023 report records a 22-foot paper-and-coconut-husk idol and a “My garbage my responsibility” theme. A garbage demon and a globe divided between ocean and waste extended the message into the visitor's route. Vijay Gohil's accompanying photograph shows the actual Ganesh, named mandal banner and physical tableaux, rather than an isolated digital portrayal.

Abhishek Teli's 2025 Marathi report names Digambar and Rajesh Mayekar for a 24-foot tissue-paper-and-rice-husk Ganesh. It describes Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam as the central concept and says young volunteers wrote the Marathi script for a presentation about family conflict and mobile-phone overuse. These details connect sculpture, stage setting and performance for one documented festival year.

sections.title: Different supports and a reuse process

paragraphs.text: The newly located press photographs extend the visible sequence back into the previous decade. They show an elephant-supported composition in 2015 and a horse-mounted form in 2016. A 2022 image adds a winged central support and two tigers. A contemporary Times of India report describes the 2022 ingredients as tissue paper and banana fibres with chalk powder and binding glue. These are individual commissions, not a single repeated design.

Pratiksha Sawant's 2026 Marathi report attributes the new 25-foot composition to Digambar and Rajesh Mayekar and describes music, knowledge and spiritual practice as its concept. It reports that pulp recovered after the previous year's immersion was combined with tissue paper, and that the mandal uses an artificial tank to collect material for another year. Those are reported workshop and immersion practices; no independent lifecycle study was found.

researchNotes.coverage: Expanded research,16 November 2026: seven located festival years (2015,2016,2022-26), six inspected Ganesh photographs, nine sources, and year-specific material/form evidence. Four new native press photographs are preserved unchanged.
gaps: No founding-era photograph or original 1989 minutes.
2024 remains a text-only year: the previously observed Daily Excelsior image URL returns 404.
2016 photograph survives in the accessible source as a small 204 px-wide portrait; no enlargement made.
Official domain remains intermittently unavailable; historical video labels do not establish dates for unrelated photos.
No open image licences found; no independent environmental testing located.
